content_of_post_to_comment: Wife just asked me “what eight books would you recommend someone read as an introduction to espionage literature” A hard question because so many of these lists reduce to greatest hits rather than a curated adventure intended to help someone fall in love with an art style. My stab in order of recommended reading: Alias Emma 1st gen Russian / British citizen smart girl chases down a Soviet hit target in London, intercepts him, and then fleas back to mi6 HQ while slav goons & English bureaucrats chase them. It's an absolute blast, read it in an afternoon. All the newcomers will read this and want more. The Day of the Jackal. A hit man takes out a target in the cold war (or tries to), and then escapes. Mayhem and fun. Still keeping the newcomers excited. The Mask of Dimitrios. Slightly more procedural and closer to “the core” of the genre in that there's less violence and more context laden conversations where both parties try to figure out what the other really knows. Mechanically a detective susses out whodunnit in the 30s across several time zones. Also, shockingly contemporary prose / energy given it was written in the 30s. The Spy Who Came in From the Cold. First true espionage story, and my only Le Carré entry (whole list could easily be Le Carré). Spy gets sent over the Berlin wall and has to get back. Intel and subterfuge and danger and violent innuendos. I didn't open with this one because i) it's old and newcomers shouldn't feel like they're in a museum ii) there are better le Carré books, but those are too involved / long to serve as genre intros A Spy Alone. One of two contemporaries to Le Carré, the pseudonymous author worked in mi6 for 25 years, then retired, and drafted a novel about an agent uncovering the Oxford spy ring. Canonically British sentiment in that the protagonist is an intellectually competent unexceptional man of feeble stature who's in truth a patriot and in love with a woman much more capable/ beautiful than he is. Every sentence of this novel advances the narrative and the prose reads effortlessly. James Bond, Casino Royale. Fleming caught something of a bad rep wrt gender, but imo Bond is not a womanizer. He's just paired with a capable and beautiful woman in each book by happenstance. Bond and awesome woman then share a near death experience, develop romantically, and then life separates them. Their separation is never even portrayed as cool, Bond is sort of tragic and Fleming knows it. Damascus Station. A former CIA analyst (David McCloskey) wrote these and you can tell, the narrative is way more functional in contrast to the British sense of linguistic beauty. The story makes up for it though with vivid and endearingly American protagonists (one commander has a full back tattoo of an eagle and a tally for each murder she avenges). Here we see an American embassy fall under in Syria. Box 88, another Brit invents a fictional joint intelligence agency between England:America. We follow a wildly competent Brit protagonist as he sorts out an Iranian plan to bomb us or something. I frankly forgot what this series debut was about because I read the other three (loved all) and mix up the timelines. Regardless it's both fun and contemporary. Couple honorable mentions that I wanted to include but couldn't are the Russian parallel series to James Bond written by Boris Akunin. It wasn't written to mimic bond, but it shares a dynamic male spy protagonist solving one off problems across a series of digestible novellas. Just super Russian sensibilities. Then there's A Perfect Spy, which is probably le Carré’s best work and deserves a few rereads.
comment: The most interesting test of an espionage primer may be whether it teaches readers to enjoy uncertainty itself. The genre’s real engine isn't secrets revealed, but the shifting belief about what is true.
